title: 11 — NoSQL Databases & Caching
html:
11 — NoSQL Databases & Caching

The senior framing: "SQL vs NoSQL" is the wrong question. The right questions are what are the access patterns, what consistency does each operation need, and what does the data shape look like. The store follows from the answers.

1. Choosing a datastore

flowchart TD
    A[New dataset] --> B{Relationships and<br/>ad-hoc queries matter?}
    B -->|Yes| C{Need horizontal write<br/>scale beyond one box?}
    C -->|No| REL[(Relational — start here)]
    C -->|Yes| D{Can you shard by a<br/>natural tenant/entity key?}
    D -->|Yes| REL2[(Sharded relational<br/>or NewSQL: Spanner, Cockroach, Yugabyte)]
    D -->|No| WIDE[(Wide-column: Cassandra, Bigtable)]
    B -->|No| E{What is the access pattern?}
    E -->|Point lookup by key| KV[(Key-value: Redis, DynamoDB)]
    E -->|Fetch a whole nested document| DOC[(Document: MongoDB, Cosmos)]
    E -->|Traverse relationships deeply| GR[(Graph: Neo4j, Neptune)]
    E -->|Time-ordered metrics| TS[(Time-series: Timescale, Influx, Prometheus)]
    E -->|Full-text / faceted search| SE[(Search: Elasticsearch, OpenSearch)]
    E -->|Aggregate over billions of rows| OLAP[(Columnar: ClickHouse, Snowflake,<br/>Synapse, DuckDB)]
    E -->|Similarity over embeddings| VEC[(Vector: pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone)]

Default position: a relational database until you have a specific, evidenced reason to add another. Postgres in particular now covers JSON documents (JSONB + GIN), full-text search, time-series (Timescale), geospatial (PostGIS), and vectors (pgvector) — one operational surface instead of five.

Polyglot persistence is real but costs real money: every store is another thing to back up, secure, monitor, upgrade, and hire for. Add one when the pain is concrete.

Store type Data model Query by Consistency default Sweet spot Bad at
Relational Tables, rows, FKs Anything (SQL) Strong (ACID) Transactions, ad-hoc queries, integrity Extreme write scale, schemaless data
Key-value key → opaque blob Key only Varies Sessions, caches, feature flags, counters Anything requiring a query
Document JSON documents Key + secondary indexes Tunable Aggregates read as a whole; varying schema Cross-document transactions, joins
Wide-column Partition key + clustering columns Key prefix + range Tunable (quorum) Massive writes, time series, per-entity feeds Ad-hoc queries, joins, aggregates
Graph Nodes + edges Traversal (Cypher/Gremlin) Usually ACID Multi-hop relationships, recommendations, fraud rings Bulk analytics, huge scale
Search Inverted index Text, facets, relevance Near-real-time Search, log analytics Being a source of truth
Time-series (series, timestamp) → values Time ranges + downsampling Eventual Metrics, IoT, market data Updates, relationships
Columnar/OLAP Columns, compressed Aggregation scans Eventual/batch Analytics over billions of rows Point updates, OLTP
Vector Embeddings ANN similarity Eventual Semantic search, RAG Exact filters at scale (use hybrid)

⚠️ The classic mistake: choosing MongoDB for relational data because "schemas are rigid". Six months later you're doing application-side joins, maintaining referential integrity by hand, and have inconsistent documents from three schema generations. Schema flexibility is a real benefit only when the schema genuinely varies per item.

2. Document databases (MongoDB / Cosmos DB)

2.1 The one rule: model for your queries

Relational modelling normalises then queries. Document modelling starts from the queries and shapes documents so each screen/API call is one read.

// Access pattern: "show an order with its lines and shipping address"
// ✔ Embed — one read, atomically consistent
{
  _id: ObjectId("..."),
  orderNumber: "ORD-2026-0042",
  customerId: ObjectId("..."),          // reference: customers are queried separately
  status: "Shipped",
  placedAt: ISODate("2026-07-20T10:14:00Z"),
  shippingAddress: { line1: "...", city: "London", postcode: "EC1A 1BB" },  // embedded VO
  lines: [                                                                  // bounded, always read together
    { sku: "ABC-1", description: "Widget", qty: 2, unitPrice: 9.99 },
    { sku: "DEF-2", description: "Gadget", qty: 1, unitPrice: 24.50 }
  ],
  total: 44.48
}

Embed vs reference:

Embed when Reference when
Read together, always Queried independently
Child has no independent identity Child is a first-class entity
The array is bounded (tens, not millions) Unbounded growth (comments, events, log lines)
Updated together (one atomic write) Updated at very different frequencies
Duplication is acceptable or desirable The data must have one authoritative copy

⚠️ The unbounded array is the #1 MongoDB design failure. Documents have a 16 MB limit, and a document with 50,000 array entries is rewritten in full on every push. Split into a separate collection with the parent's ID.

2.2 Indexing

Same B-tree principles as relational: composite index prefix rules apply (ESR: equality, sort, range). Add: multikey indexes (over arrays), text indexes, TTL indexes (auto-delete after N seconds — perfect for sessions and events), partial indexes, wildcard indexes. 🧪 db.orders.find({...}).explain("executionStats") — check totalDocsExamined vs nReturned. If they're far apart, the index isn't doing its job. A COLLSCAN on a large collection is a bug.

2.3 Consistency and transactions

  • Write concern: w:1 (primary only, fast, can lose data on failover) vs w:"majority" (durable). Use majority for anything that matters.
  • Read concern: local / majority / linearizable.
  • Read preference: primary (consistent) / secondaryPreferred (scales reads, stale).
  • Multi-document ACID transactions exist (4.0+ replica sets, 4.2+ sharded) but they're slower and contended — if you need them routinely, your document boundaries are wrong, or you should be using a relational database.

2.4 Sharding

Shard key choice is as consequential as in any distributed store: high cardinality, even distribution, and present in your common queries (otherwise every query is a scatter-gather). ⚠️ A monotonically increasing shard key (timestamp, ObjectId) creates a hot shard — all writes go to one chunk. Use a hashed shard key or a compound key with a high-cardinality prefix.

2.5 Cosmos DB (Azure-specific, relevant to your stack)

  • Request Units (RU/s) is the currency — throughput is provisioned per container or shared per database. Every operation costs RUs; a cross-partition query costs many. Budget and monitor RU consumption or the bill and the 429s will surprise you.
  • Partition key is immutable and decides everything. Logical partitions cap at 20 GB. Choose a key with high cardinality and even access.
  • Five consistency levels: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session (the default and usually correct), Consistent Prefix, Eventual. Session gives read-your-writes per client at a fraction of the cost of Strong.
  • Multi-region writes are available but require a conflict-resolution policy (LWW by default) — understand what you'll lose.

3. Wide-column (Cassandra / ScyllaDB / Bigtable)

Data model: PRIMARY KEY ((partition key), clustering column1, clustering column2). The partition key determines the node; clustering columns determine the sort order within the partition.

-- Query-first design: "get the last N messages in a conversation"
CREATE TABLE messages_by_conversation (
    conversation_id uuid,
    bucket          int,            -- e.g. yyyymm, to cap partition size
    sent_at         timestamp,
    message_id      timeuuid,
    sender_id       uuid,
    body            text,
    PRIMARY KEY ((conversation_id, bucket), sent_at, message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (sent_at DESC, message_id DESC);

Design rules:

  1. One table per query. Denormalise aggressively; duplicate data across tables. Storage is cheap, joins don't exist.
  2. Every query must include the full partition key. No partition key ⇒ a full-cluster scan (ALLOW FILTERING — a red flag in any code review).
  3. Bound partition size (< ~100 MB, < ~100k rows) with a bucketing component in the partition key.
  4. No joins, no aggregates, no transactions (lightweight transactions via Paxos exist but are slow — don't build on them).
  5. Tunable consistency per query: ONE, QUORUM, ALL. W + R > N for strong consistency (file 08 §6.4).
  6. ⚠️ Deletes create tombstones, which must be read past until compaction; a queue-like table with heavy deletes is a known Cassandra anti-pattern that eventually times out reads.

Use when: write throughput exceeds what a sharded relational cluster comfortably handles, the access pattern is a known key prefix, and you can accept eventual consistency. Don't use as a general-purpose store — the modelling constraints are severe and permanent.

4. Graph, search, time-series, columnar, vector — one paragraph each

Graph (Neo4j, Neptune, Cosmos Gremlin): use when queries are multi-hop traversals — "friends of friends who bought X", "all accounts within 3 transactions of this flagged one", permission inheritance chains, dependency/impact analysis. A 4-hop query that is a nightmare of self-joins in SQL is a one-line Cypher pattern. Don't use for bulk aggregation or as a primary transactional store for non-graph data.

Search (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch): an inverted index for full-text relevance, faceting, fuzzy matching, and log analytics. Never the source of truth — it must be rebuildable from the primary store, and that rebuild path must be exercised. Watch: mapping explosion (dynamic mapping on user-supplied JSON), shard sizing (aim ~20–50 GB per shard), and refresh interval as the freshness/throughput dial.

Time-series (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, Prometheus): optimised for append-only (series, time) → value, automatic partitioning by time, compression (10–20×), downsampling/retention policies, and time-bucketed aggregation. ⚠️ Cardinality is the constraint — every unique combination of label values is a series; putting a user ID or request ID in a label will destroy the system.

Columnar / OLAP (ClickHouse, Snowflake, Synapse, DuckDB, Parquet): stores columns contiguously, so an aggregate over 2 columns of a 200-column table reads 1% of the bytes; compression is excellent because a column is homogeneous. Use for analytics, never for point updates. DuckDB is the underrated one — an embedded OLAP engine that reads Parquet directly and pairs beautifully with Polars for local analytics (file 18).

Vector (pgvector, Qdrant, Milvus, Pinecone): stores embeddings and answers approximate nearest-neighbour queries (HNSW or IVF indexes). Powers semantic search and RAG (file 20). Key decisions: distance metric (cosine for normalised embeddings), index parameters (recall vs latency), and hybrid search — combine vector similarity with keyword/BM25 and metadata filters, because pure vector search misses exact-match intent (product codes, names, dates).

5. Redis in depth

Redis is used as a cache, but it's a data-structure server, and the structures are what make it powerful.

5.1 Structures and their canonical uses

Type Operations Use
String GET/SET/INCR/SETEX Cached JSON, counters, flags, distributed locks
Hash HGET/HSET/HINCRBY Object fields — update one field without rewriting the whole value
List LPUSH/RPOP/LRANGE/BLPOP Simple queues, recent-items feeds (capped with LTRIM)
Set SADD/SISMEMBER/SINTER Tags, unique visitors, "who's online", set algebra
Sorted set (ZSET) ZADD/ZRANGE/ZRANGEBYSCORE Leaderboards, priority queues, sliding-window rate limits, time-ordered indexes
Stream XADD/XREADGROUP/XACK Durable append-only log with consumer groups — a lightweight Kafka
HyperLogLog PFADD/PFCOUNT Approximate unique counts in 12 KB
Bitmap SETBIT/BITCOUNT Daily active users, feature flags per user ID
Geo GEOADD/GEOSEARCH Nearby-drivers, store locator
Pub/Sub PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE Fire-and-forget fan-out (⚠️ no persistence, no delivery guarantee) 
// Sliding-window rate limit with a sorted set — atomic via a single Lua script
// ZREMRANGEBYSCORE removes entries older than the window; ZCARD counts what remains
private const string SlidingWindow = """
    local key    = KEYS[1]
    local now    = tonumber(ARGV[1])
    local window = tonumber(ARGV[2])
    local limit  = tonumber(ARGV[3])
    local member = ARGV[4]

    redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', key, 0, now - window)
    local count = redis.call('ZCARD', key)
    if count < limit then
        redis.call('ZADD', key, now, member)
        redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, window)
        return 1
    end
    return 0
    """;

5.2 Operational facts that bite

  • Single-threaded command execution. One slow command blocks everyone. ⚠️ Never run KEYS *, FLUSHALL, or a large SMEMBERS in production — use SCAN with a cursor.
  • Persistence: RDB (periodic snapshot — fast restart, can lose minutes) vs AOF (append-only log — durable, slower, larger). Both, usually. If Redis holds only cache, persistence off + accept cold start is a valid choice — but then capacity-plan the origin for a cold cache.
  • Eviction policy must be set explicitly for a cache: maxmemory + allkeys-lru (or allkeys-lfu). The default noeviction returns errors on write when full — a surprising outage.
  • Every key gets a TTL unless there's a documented reason. Keyspace growth without TTLs is the standard Redis incident.
  • Key naming: app:entity:id:version — e.g. shop:portfolio:42:v3. Bumping the version invalidates a whole class atomically.
  • Cluster mode: keys are hashed to 16,384 slots. Multi-key operations require all keys in the same slot — use hash tags: {portfolio:42}:holdings and {portfolio:42}:meta co-locate.
  • Pipelining / batching: 100 round trips at 0.5 ms = 50 ms. Pipelined = ~1 ms. Batch aggressively.
  • ⚠️ Distributed locks: SET key value NX PX 30000 is the basic form. Redlock across independent nodes is contested (Kleppmann's critique: GC pauses and clock drift break the safety argument). For correctness-critical mutual exclusion, use a database constraint or a lease with a fencing token — not a Redis lock alone.
// Correct basic Redis lock: unique value + Lua-guarded release (never delete someone else's lock)
var token = Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N");
bool acquired = await db.StringSetAsync(lockKey, token, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30),
                                        When.NotExists);
// release:
const string release = """
    if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end
    """;

6. Caching strategy (the design decisions, in order)

The patterns, invalidation strategies, and failure modes (stampede, avalanche, penetration, hot key, cold start) are covered in 08_SYSTEM_DESIGN_HLD §5. This section is the decision checklist you apply when adding a cache to a real feature.

6.1 Before you add a cache

  1. Have you fixed the underlying query? A cache in front of a missing index hides the problem until the cache misses.
  2. What is the acceptable staleness? Get a number from the product owner. "Fresh" is not an answer; "up to 60 seconds" is.
  3. What is the read:write ratio? Below ~5:1, caching often isn't worth the invalidation risk.
  4. What happens on a cache miss storm? If the origin can't take 100% of traffic, you have a availability dependency, not an optimisation.
  5. Is the data user-specific? Then the cache key must include the identity, and shared HTTP caches need Vary: Authorization or Cache-Control: private.

6.2 Layer selection

Layer Latency Scope Use for
Browser/HTTP 0 One user Static assets, immutable resources
CDN 10–50 ms Global Public content, media, API GETs that are the same for everyone
In-process (IMemoryCache) ~100 ns One instance Tiny hot data, config, compiled artifacts. ⚠️ Per-instance ⇒ inconsistent across a fleet, and it consumes app memory
Distributed (Redis) 0.2–1 ms Whole fleet Sessions, shared computed results, rate-limit state
Two-tier (L1 memory + L2 Redis) best Fleet w/ local speed Hot keys; needs invalidation broadcast (Redis pub/sub)
Database result cache / materialised view varies DB Expensive aggregates

.NET note: HybridCache (.NET 9) implements the L1+L2 pattern with stampede protection built in — prefer it over hand-rolling IMemoryCache + IDistributedCache.

6.3 What to cache

Good candidates Bad candidates
Expensive to compute, cheap to store Cheap to compute
Read far more than written Write-heavy
Tolerant of staleness Money balances, inventory counts, permissions (unless very short TTL)
Shared across users Data unique to one request
Reference/lookup data Large blobs (use object storage + CDN)

⚠️ Caching authorisation decisions is a recurring security bug: a revoked permission stays effective for the TTL. If you must, keep the TTL in seconds and support explicit invalidation on revocation.

7. Data consistency across stores

The moment you have two stores (DB + cache, DB + search, DB + warehouse), you have a dual-write problem: two writes cannot be atomic without a distributed transaction.

flowchart LR
    A[App] -->|1. write| DB[(Primary DB)]
    A -->|2. write| S[(Search index)]
    A -.->|❌ crash between 1 and 2| X[Permanently inconsistent]

Solutions, best to worst:

  1. Transactional outbox — write the business change and an outbox row in one transaction; a relay publishes to the other systems. Reliable, and the standard answer.
  2. CDC (Change Data Capture) — Debezium/SQL Server CDC/logical replication tails the transaction log and emits changes. No application code; captures every writer, including manual fixes.
  3. Cache-aside with TTL — accept bounded staleness; the TTL is the self-healing mechanism.
  4. Dual write with compensation/reconciliation — write both, plus a periodic job that detects and repairs drift.
  5. ❌ Dual write with no safety net — works until the first crash or timeout.

Always add reconciliation for anything financial or customer-visible: a scheduled job that compares the two stores and reports drift. Assume divergence will happen; the question is whether you detect it.

8. Cost, capacity, and operations

Consideration Question to answer before choosing
Sizing Working set in RAM? (Redis must fit; a DB benefits from it)
Growth Storage in 3 years at current write rate × retention
Throughput Peak ops/s vs the store's realistic per-node ceiling
Backup/restore RPO/RTO, and how long a full restore actually takes at your data size
Upgrade path Rolling upgrade support; downtime per major version
Multi-region Replication model and conflict resolution
Managed vs self-hosted Managed is almost always right unless you have a platform team
Cost model Per-GB, per-RU, per-node, per-query — model your actual workload, not the marketing number
Skills Who on the team can debug it at 3am?

9. Checklist & self-test

Adding a new datastore — checklist

  • Access patterns written down before the schema
  • Partition/shard key chosen for cardinality, distribution, and query alignment; immutability considered
  • Consistency requirement stated per operation
  • Every query covered by an index; verified with explain
  • Partition/document/row size bounded; growth capped
  • TTL/retention policy defined
  • Backup, restore, and a tested restore drill
  • Monitoring: latency percentiles, error rate, memory/RU/CPU, replication lag, eviction rate, hit ratio
  • Consistency with the primary store: outbox/CDC + reconciliation
  • Failure behaviour defined: what does the app do when this store is down?
  • Security: auth, TLS, network isolation, encryption at rest, least privilege

🔍 Questions to test yourself

  • When would you choose NoSQL over relational? When the access pattern is a known key, the data shape is a self-contained aggregate or genuinely variable, and you need write scale or geographic distribution beyond what a single relational cluster gives — and you can accept losing joins, ad-hoc queries, and (usually) multi-record transactions.
  • Embed or reference? Read-together + bounded + updated-together ⇒ embed. Independent identity or unbounded growth ⇒ reference.
  • Why is my Cassandra query slow? Almost certainly missing the partition key (scatter-gather), an oversized partition, or tombstones.
  • How do you keep a cache consistent with the database? You don't, exactly — you bound staleness with TTLs, invalidate after commit on the write paths you own, and use CDC/outbox where correctness demands it. Then you state the staleness window as a product decision.
  • How do you handle a cache stampede? Per-key loader lock or single-flight, jittered TTLs, stale-while-revalidate, and probabilistic early expiry.
  • Is Redis a database? It can be (persistence + replication), but treating it as the system of record means accepting a durability model most teams haven't actually read. Usually: cache and ephemeral state.
  • What's the risk of a two-tier cache? L1 instances diverge; you need an invalidation broadcast, and you must accept a window where different users see different data.
